A few months ago I was talking to my musician buddy and I asked him when his next album would drop and he responded, "I have no interest in dropping an album because nobody listens to full length albums anymore". I was shocked because I've never heard a musician openly state having no interest in creating a cohesive project. So I asked to learn more about this theory and his reasoning was simple, he believes that in this modern age of music streaming these new streaming platforms like Spotify, Google Play Music, Pandora and etc., people are becoming more conditioned to quickly check out a playlist that fits their mood as opposed to listening to an album featuring only one artist or band. He went on to say that as an indie musician it is more economically efficient to periodically drop a single with the plan of it being featured in a playlist created by other people. Right away that made a lot of sense to me because I have lately noticed that most of the music I discover are via playlists created by music heads I trust. I decided to test this theory by last week adding a page of playlists to my website using music uploaded by artists from around the world (a shuffle button will be added next week). I also tried to make these playlists not so generic by thinking of creative themes for each playlist. Right away I noticed a lot more people listening to music on the website compared to before I added to playlists to it. In fact now users are creating playlists of their own and other users have been listening to them as well. So after a week of this experiment I have noticed lots of positive feedback and reviews. My goal is to build a community of users that will feature musicians uploading music and the listeners curating their favorite songs into creatively themed public playlists because after week one I'm pretty excited about what will happen. Now I'm wondering is there even a point for albums in this era because to me playlists seem to be the future. What do you think?

I'd say you're right on the money about albums being passé again. It comes and goes with the times. You could argue that classical symphonies are the original concept albums. Before that, music was mostly released piece by piece, ("singles") in the form of sheet music and live performances.

More recently the advent of FM radio, affordable turntables and personal recording devices enabled and popularized the "playlist" concept, even as albums were considered the most relevant and established format. By the mid 1970's artists were in peak "concept album" mode, yet the dancefloor and radio DJs of the time took pride in promoting obscure album cuts, "creating" new hit songs in the process.

This synergy between albums and playlists lasted until the next major distribution method was developed on the internet, disrupting the album paradigm to the point where it has become mostly irrelevant. I too, like most of us now, prefer to compile playlists of individual songs, often from a variety of artists.

My playlists have evolved from hand written cassette compilations recorded from live radio broadcasts, to carefully annotated CD's full of new and rare music gleaned from the early days of peer-to-peer filesharing, to most recently settling on the cloud of shared music on YouTube.

You are welcome to browse my personal YT "DJ" mix. It's just for personal use, I don't promote it (I think YT ads are too disruptive), but it is convenient to assemble and use on a variety of devices.

What is an album, if not just a kind of playlist itself? It can't have the kind of diversity a normal playlist can, since everything comes from the same artist, but the thought and curation that goes into a good album—the songs and their order—can put an album leagues ahead of a shuffled library.

There seems to be a strong leaning towards albums in the responses. I very much enjoy full albums, and I suspect that people who prefer albums also have a strong loyalty towards bands they like. If I discover a band that is new to me, and if they have more than one album, I will try to find copies of the other albums.

Occasionally I will listen to a playlist on shuffle, usually with a "smart" playlist based on a window of time. Quite often the result of this is I discover there are gaps in my collection, I hear a song I used to like but haven't been following the group for a while, or never listened to their earlier stuff. So playlists and shuffle tend to lead me back to listening to albums.

An exception to this is EDM, where most releases only exist only as "tracks", and sometimes even the artist names will be limited to a tiny handful of releases. Some artists go to the trouble of producing EPs or even full length albums, but for others doing so is an unacceptable form of "selling out". Fortunately DJ sets exist as a way to compensate for this, although the individual tracks become a little more anonymous.
